problems.description: Frontmatter interface gains a `[key: string]: unknown` index signature and every raw frontmatter field is spread into each Page, loosening the previously curated/typed contract and pushing untyped data downstream to template consumers.
TemplateEngine is instantiated and loaded eagerly on every build even when no page references a template, coupling render() to an engine the common path may not use.
SonarQube delta shows cognitive complexity +36 and duplications +4.1%; the new frontmatter parse loop and template rendering path duplicate escaping/layout logic previously centralized in layout().

handlebars is promoted to runtime dependencies (correct, since it is now required at build runtime), but its transitive lockfile entries (minimist, neo-async, source-map, uglify-js, wordwrap) are correctly re-flagged as non-dev.
No test files appear in the diff for the new TemplateEngine or the modified build/frontmatter/render paths.

strengths: Coherent feature design: per-page `template`/`layout` frontmatter keys with a clean new `src/templates.ts` module, exported through index.ts following the existing barrel pattern.
Removes the hardcoded `layout()` HTML string from render.ts in favor of data-driven templates, reducing hardcoding and enabling user-defined layouts.
Non-template frontmatter keys are preserved generically, so the engine can accept arbitrary data without schema churn per feature.
commit_reviews.summary: A reasonable, well-scoped template-engine feature that replaces the hardcoded layout and slots into the existing module structure, offset by a type-safety regression (wildcard Frontmatter + raw data spread into Page), +36 cognitive complexity / +4.1% duplication, and no added tests — and note the 0.60 convention score appears noisy since the flagged violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE/snake_case on untouched cache.ts/cli.ts) contradict standard TypeScript conventions, so I grounded the score in the measurement while flagging the discrepancy.

problems.description: @types/chokidar@^1.7.5 is a deprecated stub describing the v1 API while chokidar@3.6.0 (which bundles its own v3 types) is the runtime dependency — the type versions are mismatched and can mask or corrupt type-checking for the watcher.

Measurement reports 69 convention violations (snake_case functions, non-PascalCase classes/interfaces, lowercase constants) in build.ts/cache.ts/cli.ts — but build.ts and cache.ts do not exist in this commit's tree, so the scan is stale or from another story; cli.ts (actually modified here) uses camelCase functions and UPPER_CASE constants.

SonarQube cognitive complexity +32 and smells +3: serve.ts bundles HTTP static serving, WebSocket broadcast, chokidar watching, and rebuild coalescing into one module; the request-handling and rebuild logic could be factored into smaller units.
parseArgs does not validate --port (Number.parseInt on arbitrary input yields NaN, which then fails at server.listen), and cli.ts has no --host flag even though ServeOptions exposes host.

strengths: The serve/live-reload integration reuses the existing build() and BuildOptions from ssg.ts instead of re-implementing generation — clean architectural seam for the story's integration session.
New functionality isolated in a dedicated src/serve.ts module with 216 lines of tests added (5/5 passing in the inspected cell); proper jest/ts-jest usage consistent with the repo's test layout.
Rebuild is debounced (50ms) with a rebuilding/pending coalescing flag, avoiding rebuild storms under rapid file changes.
Security-aware: path traversal guard (filePath.startsWith(outputDir + path.sep)) plus 403/404 handling in the static server.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid 'integration' commit that cleanly wires a live-reload dev server (chokidar + ws) into the existing build pipeline with good tests; the main blemishes are the stale @types/chokidar dependency and a convention-scan result that references files (build.ts/cache.ts) absent from this commit, so the 0.60 convention score should be treated cautiously.

problems.description: 69 naming-convention violations across build.ts, cache.ts, cli.ts (Classes/Interfaces should use PascalCase, Constants UPPER_CASE, Functions not snake_case); convention score 0.60 falls well short of a healthy refactor.

Silent error swallowing in loadConfig() and resolvePluginEntry() (`catch { continue }` / return []) means a misconfigured config or plugin path fails invisibly with no diagnostic, making debugging harder.
Cognitive complexity +94 with nested try/catch, recursive flattenPluginExport, and multi-candidate resolvePluginPath — the config/plugin resolver is more complex than the code it replaces.
resolvePluginEntry silently returns [] for BUILTIN_PLUGIN_NAMES and unresolvable paths, so a typo'd or unsupported plugin string is dropped without warning instead of failing loudly.

strengths: build.ts shrinks from 86 to 33 lines; config loading and plugin resolution are extracted into dedicated modules (config.ts, engine.ts) with clear typed interfaces (BuildInput, SsgConfig).
Idiomatic config system via defineConfig/normalizeConfig with robust multi-format discovery (ts/mts/js/cjs/mjs/json) mirroring established SSG/tooling patterns.
Flexible plugin loading that flattens functions, objects, arrays, and module paths into a normalized Plugin[] list, enabling clean extension points.
commit_reviews.summary: A directionally sound architectural refactor that decouples config/plugin concerns from the build orchestrator, but it ships with heavy convention violations (69, score 0.60), +94 cognitive complexity, and silent-failure error handling that offset the structural gains.

problems.description: CachedPage overlaps Page with redundant/ambiguous fields (contentHtml, content, html all present) and cachedToPage() is a manual mapping layer that can drift out of sync with Page as the domain model evolves.

Incremental correctness keys only on sourceHash + templateHash; plugin-derived output (Plugin API) is not hashed, so a plugin whose behavior changes without touching sources/templates will serve stale cached pages.
The new cache module (hash logic, manifest round-trip, skip-vs-rebuild decision) has no test coverage visible in the diff despite being the most bug-prone new logic.
hashFile() swallows read errors and returns '', silently degrading cache invalidation instead of surfacing the failure.

Discrepancy flagged per instructions: the reported 69 convention violations (score 0.60) appear to be analyzer false positives — the diff uses PascalCase classes/interfaces (BuildResult, CachedPage, CacheManager), UPPER_CASE constants (CACHE_VERSION, CACHE_FILENAME, TEMPLATE_EXTS), and camelCase functions throughout, matching the repo's existing TypeScript style.

strengths: Backward-compatible API: build() is preserved as a thin wrapper over buildWithStats(), so existing callers and the serve command are unaffected.
Follows the established module-per-concern layout and reuses existing types (Page, BuildOptions, Frontmatter, Plugin, SsgConfig) rather than inventing parallel abstractions.
Sound invalidation design: deterministic sha256 over a sorted, recursively collected template tree makes the manifest reproducible across runs.
Cleanly isolates the feature behind --incremental/--clean CLI flags with an opt-in default, and measurably reduces duplication (-0.7%).
commit_reviews.summary: Well-fitted, backward-compatible incremental-build feature that slots into the existing engine/plugin architecture with clean conventions as written — the low mechanical convention score (0.60) looks like a misconfigured-analyzer false positive, since the diff consistently uses correct PascalCase/camelCase/UPPER_CASE, with only minor cache-correctness and test-coverage concerns worth addressing.

compounding_issues: Session 1 committed compiled dist/ output (and package-lock/node_modules churn) into git; dist/ artifacts carry through all 5 sessions, bloating every diff (session 1 files_changed=5306) and polluting the repo.

Session 3's live-reload dev server was built monolithically in serve.ts, forcing session 4 to fully rewrite it into the DevServerPlugin (build.ts shrank 86->33 lines, serve.ts was split) — integration had to be reworked rather than extended.
The seed codebase (an unrelated Auth API, early_degrade condition) was effectively discarded by session 1's greenfield build, so no carryover value from the tier2 seed.

Session 2's template engine and session 1's render.ts both own HTML emission, leaving overlapping render responsibilities (render.ts coexists with TemplatePlugin) that the refactor only partially consolidated.
key_decisions: Plugin lifecycle-hook architecture (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd) in session 4 — markdown, template, and dev-server were all absorbed as plugins, making session 5's incremental engine extension trivial.
SsgEngine core class with per-build stats and a build context (config, cwd, options) — separated engine from CLI/build entry points and enabled incremental skip metrics.
SHA-256 hash-based incremental cache (.ssg-cache.json manifest) with template-directory hash invalidation, wired into the engine as the session-5 cross-cutting feature.
Handlebars template engine with per-page frontmatter template selection (default template + fallback), built in session 2 and preserved through refactor.
Config loader (loadConfig/loadConfigFile/resolvePlugins) supporting an ssg config file, introduced in the refactor to unify build and serve entry points.
chokidar + ws live-reload dev server (session 3) with rebuild debouncing and WebSocket reload broadcast.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and non-monotonically. Session 1 produced a clean, working greenfield SSG (monolithic build.ts, 1/1 tests passing) that served as a sound foundation. Sessions 2 and 3 layered real features — a Handlebars template engine (2/2 tests) and a chokidar/ws live-reload dev server (3/3 tests) — but accumulated structural weight in build.ts and serve.ts. Session 4 was the pivotal refactor: a plugin system with lifecycle hooks plus a dedicated SsgEngine core, which cut build.ts from 86 to 33 lines and folded markdown/template/devServer into plugins while keeping all 3 tests green. Session 5 then exploited that architecture to deliver the largest feature (incremental builds + hash cache, engine rewritten, 4/4 tests) at lower cost ($0.033 vs $0.052) and shorter duration (302s vs 614s) than the refactor itself — evidence the refactor paid off. Across the arc, tests monotonically grew 1->2->3->3->4 with zero retries, cache hit rate held ~0.94-0.96, and confidence stayed at 1.0.
story_review.summary: A near-textbook story arc — greenfield to feature growth to a well-timed plugin refactor to a cross-cutting incremental-build capstone — where the session-4 refactor demonstrably enabled a cheaper, faster session 5, marred only by committed build artifacts and a dev server that needed rework rather than extension.
